canonical_statement: The study evaluates whether white-box, black-box consistency, and reflexive uncertainty-quantification methods developed for single-turn language-model outputs remain useful for predicting success of multi-turn LLM-agent trajectories.
The evaluation uses four multi-turn tool-use datasets: 200 BFCL-v4 tasks and 114 retail, 50 airline, and 114 telecom tasks from tau2-bench.

Completed trajectories are labeled with each benchmark's binary success reward based on state, response, required-action, or related task checks, and this binary label is the prediction target for uncertainty scoring.

outcome.definition: Binary benchmark reward for completed trajectory

canonical_statement: Five scored agent models are evaluated: gpt-4o-mini, gpt-oss-20b, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3.5-9B, and MiniMax-M3.

For each task the study records one greedy reference trajectory at temperature 0 with top-5 token log probabilities and three additional sampled trajectories at temperature 0.7 for black-box consistency measurement.
White-box scores are computed over the committed action-token span of each agent turn rather than over the full generation or reasoning tokens.
Cross-turn white-box aggregation includes first, last, arithmetic mean, minimum, and position-weighted early and late combinations of per-turn confidence.

The black-box consistency family includes final-message non-contradiction probability, first-action consistency, action-set consistency, action-distribution consistency, action-edit consistency, and trajectory-equivalence rate.
Non-Contradiction Probability compares the reference and sampled final messages using bidirectional contradiction probabilities from microsoft/deberta-large-mnli.
First-Action Consistency is the fraction of sampled trajectories whose first action type matches the reference trajectory's first action type.
Action-Set Consistency is the mean Jaccard similarity between the unique action-type sets of the reference and sampled trajectories.
Action-Distribution Consistency is one minus the mean Jensen-Shannon divergence between action-type frequency distributions of the reference and sampled trajectories.
Action-Edit Consistency is one minus normalized Levenshtein edit distance between ordered action-type sequences, making it sensitive to action order and trajectory length.

Trajectory Equivalence Rate uses gemini-flash-lite to judge whether each sampled full trajectory reaches the same task-relevant outcome as the reference trajectory without showing the judge the hidden task instructions or reward.
The P(True) reflexive scorer asks the scored model whether its trajectory succeeded and uses the probability assigned to the TRUE token as confidence.

The verbalized-confidence reflexive scorer asks the model for a Yes/No success judgment and the probability that the judgment is correct, converting a No judgment to success confidence by taking its complement.
AUROC is the primary discrimination metric; the study also reports task-clustered bootstrap uncertainty, AUPRC, selective-prediction prediction rejection ratio, and expected calibration error.
For tau2-bench, the simulated user is fixed to gpt-4.1-mini at temperature 0 to minimize simulator-side sampling variance.

The SAUP-inspired propagation controls are adaptations to action-level traces rather than faithful reproductions of SAUP because the recorded traces lack clean ReAct thought spans and step-level situational labels.
The study uses a text-action interface as a measurement surface so committed action tokens are observable and carry comparable token log probabilities across the evaluated model/provider stack.
Across model-dataset cells, scorer rankings under AUPRC and PRR closely agree with AUROC rankings, with median Spearman correlations of 0.94 and 0.95, respectively.

population.label: Model-dataset cells across BFCL-v4 and tau2-bench

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Median Spearman rank correlation 0.94 with AUPRC and 0.95 with PRR

canonical_statement: For columns with at least 20 minority-class trajectories, the 95% task-clustered bootstrap intervals around main AUROC estimates have median half-width 0.10.

population.label: Model-domain columns with at least 20 minority-class trajectories

canonical_statement: The largest tau2-bench white-box AUROC point estimate is 0.725 for SP with mean aggregation on Qwen3.5-9B telecom; changing the aggregation for the same base score can reduce AUROC to about 0.228.
Across the full white-box grid, 91 of 240 model-dataset-scorer cells have AUROC below 0.5.
Twenty-one of the 240 white-box cells have 95% bootstrap intervals lying entirely below AUROC 0.5.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: Cells with interval entirely below AUROC 0.5

canonical_statement: For gpt-4o-mini, LNSP with minimum aggregation has AUROC 0.72 on retail but 0.24 on telecom, illustrating model-domain dependence of the same white-box aggregation rule.

population.label: gpt-4o-mini on tau2 retail and telecom

canonical_statement: For gpt-4o-mini, LNSP-minimum selective prediction has PRR 0.44 on retail but -0.28 on telecom.

population.label: gpt-4o-mini on tau2 retail and telecom

canonical_statement: The strongest SAUP-inspired propagation control averages 0.434 AUROC across the 15 tau2 model-domain cells, below the best fixed naive aggregation at 0.53.
On BFCL-v4, action- or trajectory-level consistency reaches approximately 0.71 to 0.77 AUROC for four of the five evaluated models.
Trajectory Equivalence Rate reaches 0.868 AUROC for Qwen3.5-9B on tau2-airline.
Action-Set Consistency reaches 0.819 AUROC for gpt-oss-20b on tau2-airline.
Trajectory Equivalence Rate falls to 0.342 AUROC for gpt-4o-mini on tau2-telecom, where the greedy trajectory success rate is 11%.
On BFCL-v4, P(True) AUROC ranges from about 0.746 to 0.852 across the five scored models.
Across tau2-bench, the best reflexive AUROC reported by domain is 0.710 on retail, 0.852 on telecom, and 0.703 on airline.

Qwen3.5-9B and MiniMax-M3 each succeed on 74% of airline tasks, yet Qwen3.5-9B has weak reflexive AUROC while MiniMax-M3 retains a stronger P(True) signal, showing that reflexive-scorer usefulness does not track task success rate directly.
At the family level, action consistency has mean peak-per-cell AUROC 0.705, reflexive scoring 0.691, judged consistency 0.686, white-box scoring 0.628, and message consistency 0.603.

outcome.measurement_method: Mean of family highest AUROC per cell

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Action consistency 0.705; reflexive 0.691; judged consistency 0.686; white-box 0.628; message consistency 0.603

canonical_statement: The gemini-flash-lite judge used by TER adds approximately $0.002 per task beyond the cost of sampled trajectories.
In the agent-only prefix-conditioned airline ablation with gpt-4o-mini, the best local next-action consistency score reaches only 0.588 AUROC.

Against database-state ground truth on retail and airline, the trajectory-equivalence judge attains precision 0.88, recall 0.93, and F1 0.90 over 1,365 judged pairs with determinate database-state equivalence.

population.label: Determinate retail and airline trajectory pairs

canonical_statement: Replacing gemini-flash-lite with gemini-flash on airline yields 91% judge agreement (Cohen kappa 0.81) and changes TER AUROC by 0.021 on average and at most 0.062 across the five models.

population.label: Airline trajectory pairs across five scored models

canonical_statement: Increasing sampled trajectories from m=1 to m=3 raises mean TER AUROC across the 15 tau2 model-domain cells from 0.63 to 0.68; on airline the mean rises from 0.62 to 0.69.
For Qwen3.5-9B on airline, TER AUROC increases from 0.76 at one sampled draw to 0.87 at three sampled draws.
Across tau2-bench trajectory pairs, TER averages 0.95 for success-success pairs but 0.40 for failure-failure pairs; on airline the corresponding values are 0.87 and 0.37.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: All tau2 success-success 0.95; failure-failure 0.40; airline 0.87 and 0.37

canonical_statement: In tau2 retail with gpt-4o-mini, native tool calling succeeds on 46 of 114 greedy tasks (40.4%) versus 42 of 114 (36.8%) with the text-action interface; the 3.5 percentage-point difference is not significant at the 5% level.
In the same retail interface ablation, TER AUROC is 0.759 with text actions and 0.761 with native tool calling, while AEC is 0.678 and 0.681, respectively.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: TER 0.759 text-action vs 0.761 native; AEC 0.678 vs 0.681

canonical_statement: In the retail interface ablation, NCP AUROC decreases from 0.762 with text actions to 0.716 with native tool calling.

Simple negated trajectory turn-count and tool-call-count baselines can themselves predict success substantially above chance in some tau2 model-domain cells, including turn-count AUROC 0.83 for Qwen2.5-7B telecom.

On airline, the highest observed consistency AUROC exceeds the highest observed reflexive AUROC for all five scored models, but only the Qwen3.5-9B paired difference cleanly excludes zero: 0.438 with 95% interval 0.244 to 0.614.

Within the airline consistency family, TER is the highest-AUROC scorer for three models, ASC is highest for gpt-oss-20b, and AEC is highest for MiniMax-M3, so judged trajectory equivalence does not uniformly dominate symbolic consistency.
Calibration is uneven across reflexive scorers and model-domain cells; some telecom cells have low ECE while several airline and telecom combinations are substantially miscalibrated.
No uncertainty-quantification family or individual scorer is uniformly reliable across the evaluated models and domains.
White-box action-token confidence is not a reliable drop-in trajectory-level uncertainty method unless the cross-turn aggregation rule is validated for the target model and domain.
Reflexive scoring is presented as the lowest-cost broadly useful practical baseline when a pre-outcome transcript self-assessment is acceptable.

Sampled-trajectory consistency is most attractive when repeated runs are already in the evaluation budget, pass-at-k style sampling is needed for another reason, or a high-stakes setting can afford extra trajectories for stronger failure ranking.
The authors recommend future work with step-level labels, experiments that act on per-turn uncertainty during execution, and evaluation on additional agent environments such as web-browsing tasks.
The authors recommend per-deployment validation rather than assuming uncertainty signals transfer safely across models and domains.

The benchmark scope is limited to the BFCL-v4 multi-turn subset and three tau2-bench text domains; generalization to other tool-use benchmarks, web agents, embodied agents, and more open-ended tasks is untested.

The trajectory-success target is benchmark reward and can contain label noise from database-state, assertion, action, and final-message checks; this noise limits attainable discrimination and can distort calibration.

Because full sampled trajectories resample the simulated user together with the agent, black-box consistency measures variability of the joint agent-user system rather than agent uncertainty in isolation.

White-box findings depend on the text-action interface used to expose action-token probabilities; the native tool-calling robustness check covers only gpt-4o-mini on retail and does not establish cross-model interface invariance.
Per-domain task counts are modest, especially airline with 50 tasks, producing wide bootstrap intervals and leaving many within-column scorer rankings unresolved.

Trajectory Equivalence Rate depends on a single external judge model; the study validates it against database-state ground truth and one larger-judge swap but does not test every domain or more distant judge families.

The study scores committed action spans and completed-trajectory success; observation uncertainty, reasoning-token uncertainty, step-level labels by action/tool type, and online use of uncertainty for abstention, clarification, or escalation are outside scope.

All evaluated uncertainty signals are measured after completed trajectories, so the experiments do not establish that using these signals as mid-run safety gates would prevent harmful or irreversible actions.
